purpose: Catch macro placement, power-strategy, and IO/escape routability problems before placement commits them to a database that takes days. Once macro placement is locked, a wrong channel width between macros costs a placement restart; a missing power-decap strategy costs an IR-drop re that touches metal stack choices; order costs a package redesign.

checks: Show the macro placement with channels annotated to the worst-case routing congestion you saw at the previous node, me which channels are tighter than the routing resource estimator budget.
checks.evidence_demanded: Floorplan view with macro + channels + a congestion overlay (or the tool's routing-resource estimator map). The reviewer looks for channels< 2x the sum of estimated feedthrough tracks.
checks.red_flag: 'All channels look fine' without a congestion overlay, or an overlay where the worst channel is <1.5x the budget on a 28nm planar node — at 7nm/5nm you want >2x because pin accessibility and double/triple patterning add variance.
checks.why_it_matters: A tight channel that placements into a routable solution at floorplan time becomes unroutable at route-opt because routing adds track detour overhead the estimator didn't model. Cost: 2-4 week placement restart with degraded QoR.

checks.question: Walk me through the power strategy: how many power rails, what domain, where do the bump/pad pitches force stripes to land, and what-case IR-drop target at the worst corner?
checks.evidence_demanded: Power intent (CPF/UPF) view, the package/bump map overlay, and an early IR-drop estimate from the power-integr. The reviewer wants the IR-drop number next to the targete.g., 'worst 35 mV on VDD at ss/125C/0.9V, target 50 mV').
checks.red_flag: No power-integrity co-analysis, or 'we'll fix it after placement' as a strategy. On 7nm and IR-drop is the dominant closure problem and a power strategy designed post-placement touches theN mesh shape which is set in Mx layers.
checks.why_it_matters: Late IR-drop fixes require either widening straps (which costs routability) or adding decap (which costs area and leakage). On FinFET nodes, decap efficiency at the SoC level by the FinFET decap density per um^2, so the only knob is strap widening — and costs routing tracks.

checks.question: Show the IO pin order and the package substrate escape plan. Are bump/pad assignments matched to the package breakout, or is there a long escape that crosses the chip diagonally?
checks.evidence_demanded: Bump map aligned with the package ball map and the escape routing plan from the package team. Critical: signal integrity group ordering (e.g., DDR byte-lane ordering must preserve fly-by matching within the package).
checks.red_flag: Pin order swapped from feasibility review without sign, or a signal-integrity-critical group (DDRDes) reassigned without the SI team's review. At 28nm you can sometimes rescue with-bonding tricks; at 7nm flip-chip4 bumps, a wrong assignment is a package re-spin.
checks.why_it_matters: Wrong pin order forces a package redesign (cost: $1M+ and weeks) or, worse, an SI failure that masquerades as a timing issue downstream.

checks.question: : placement of always-on cells, retentionops, and level shifters, and are the always-on rails to their regions cleanly?
checks.evidence_demanded: Power intent view with always-on islands and retention/isolation, plus a check that the always-on rail every always-on cell without crossing a switched power domain.
checks.red_flag: An always-on cell placed in a switched-power region with no isolation cell in series, or a level shifter missing at a domain crossing. At 28nm this is recoverable; at 7nm and below with multi-VDD isolation is a functional failure.
checks.why_it_matters: Powerent errors caught at floorplan cost a re-pl Caught at pre-CTS they cost a partial re-placement plus a UPF rewrite. Caught at pre-tapeout they cost.

checks.question: Are the blockage layers and routing halos applied correctly around macros, IP boundaries, and noise-sensitive analog regions?
checks.Floorplan view with blockage and halo la: Missing halos around analog IP (noise coupling substrate), or a halo too tight to prevent buffering at the IP boundary. At 28nm a missing halo SI issues; at 5nm with backside PDN, missing halos around analog can cause substrate noise coupling that no tool catches until measurement.
checks.why_it_matters: Analog IP performance is destroyed by digital switching noise injected through the substrate. The halo is the cheapest insurance and the most commonly forgotten.

checks: Pre-CTS hold-fixing report showing buffer count by region, plus the utilization map after hold-fix. The reviewer looks for hold buffers clustered in high-utilization areas.
red_flag: Hold-fixing pushing any 75% utilization at 28nm or over 65% at 7nm, or hold buffers inserted inside macro channels (they will block routing later).
why_it_matters: Hold fixing is supposed to be cheap at pre-CTS. If it isn't, the placement has long combinational paths that CTS will make worse, and the only fix is a placement rebuild.

question: What is the placement QoR on the key interfaces (top-10 critical paths, top-10 long-combinational paths, top-10 endpoints by slack)?
evidence_demanded: Timing report paths with the cell-by-cell breakdown. The reviewer walks the paths to see: cell types, net lengths, layer assignments, fanout. Looking for: long nets (>500 um at 28nm, >100 um at 7nm), high-fanout nets, layer-hopping.
red_flag: A 'critical' path dominated by long wire delay rather than cell delay. That means the placer hasn't pushed the flops close enough and CTS pessimism will kill the path. A path with >4 layer hops in the at 7nm is also a flag.
why_it_matters: Wire-dominated critical paths are the ones that get worse with every subsequent step (CTS pessimism, route detour, SI delay). Cell-dominated paths are the ones that get fixed by ECO.

question: Are the macro clock pins reachable, and is there a documented CTS strategy for each macro (skew group, balance group, ignore)?
Clock planning document with each clocke: A clocked macro with no skew specification, or skew groups defined in the planning doc that don't appear in the SDC. At 28nm missing this causes timing closure grief; at 7nm it causes CTS to fail outright or unusable skew.
why_it_matters: Clocked macros interact with the logic clock tree; if the SDC doesn't say how, the tool guesses. The guess is usually wrong and surfaces as setup violations at pre-tapeout sign when the schedule is gone.

question: What does-drop analysis look like at this stage, and are there any hotspots that placement should have mitigated but didn't?
evidence_demanded: Early IR-drop map from the power-integrity team overlaid on the placement. The reviewer looks for hotspots coincident with high-switching regions (clock-gen, CPU cores, SerDes) and whether the floorplan's power strap plan is reaching those regions.
red_flag: A hotspot > 10DD at the worst corner, or hotspots in regions that were 'reserved for straps' at floorplan but the straps don't actually reach them in the placement. At 7 below, dynamic IR-drop hotspots are a sign of a placement-quality problem.
why_it_matters: IR-drop fix at this stage is a placement tweak (spread the hot region, add local decap). IR-drop fix at signoff is a power-strap and decap ECO that touches the metal stack.

question the scan stitch look like? Are the scan chains balanced, and is the scan-enabled signal reachable without crossing bad regions?
evidence_demanded: Scan chain report with chain lengths, scan_enable, and the scan hookup congestion. The reviewer looks for unbalanced chains (>2x the average) and chains that route through congested regions.
red_flag: Scan chains > 2x the average length, or scan_enable routed as a high-fanout net through a congested region. At 28nm this is a routing nuisance; at 5nm it's a congestion disaster because scan_enable is in every flop.
why_it_matters: Bad scan stitch causes routing congestion that masquerades as a logic-routing problem and forces unnecessary placement spreading.

question: Has the routing layer assignment been planned, and are the critical nets on the correct layers?
evidence_demanded: Layer assignment strategy from the routing team, with critical-path layer assignments visible. The reviewer checks that long critical nets are on upper layers (lower R) and short critical nets are not wasting upper-layer tracks.
red_flag: Critical paths on the lowest metal layers, or upper-layer congestion in critical-path regions that the placer didn't reserve for. At 28nm you have 6-7 routing layers; at 5nm you have 15+ and the layer assignment matters enormously.
why_it_matters: Wrong layer assignment is the #1 silent QoR killer. The placer can place perfectly and the router can route cleanly, and the design is still slow because the critical nets are on the wrong layers.

kill_questions: Where is the setup-slack histogram wall, and how many endpoints are below zero? (Wall at −200 ps or worse stops the review.)
Show me the worst congestion region and tell me what placement is doing about it. (If the answer is 'CTS/route will fix it,' the review stops because CTS/route won't.)
waiver_culture: Hold-fixing impact on utilization gets waved through when the timing wall is acceptable, and the waiver later costs 1-2 weeks of hold-fixing congestion at route-opt that requires local placement spreading.

confidence.purpose: Confirm timing is actually closed across all corners and modes with extracted parasitics, that the ECOs that were applied didn't introduce new violations, and that the signoff corner set is complete. This is the last gate before mask-making; everything caught here either fixes by ECO (cheap if OCV margin exists) or forces a re-spin (expensive).

checks.question: Show me the signoff corner set and the mode coverage, and tell me which corners are checked at which voltages and temperatures.
checks.evidence_demanded: Corner matrix document with signoff-tagged corners (typically ss/0.81V/-40C, ss/0.81V/125C, ff/0.9V/-40C, ff/0.9V/125C, plus typ for SI, plus ss/0.9V/125C for hold, plus any custom corners for IR-drop). Mode coverage: functional, scan, BIST, DFT shift, mission-mode for the application.
checks.red_flag: A corner missing from the signoff set — especially hold at the cold corner (ss/-40C is the worst for hold, not the worst for setup), or a missing IR-drop corner at 7nm and below where dynamic drop is a real setup issue.
checks.why_it_matters: A missing corner means silicon will fail at that corner in production. The most common miss: hold at cold, which only shows up at low-temperature test or in the field.

checks.question: Show me the setup and hold slack distribution across all signoff corners, and tell me the global skew and OCV margin.
